notes: Consistently attributed to R. Buckminster Fuller across quotation collections and Fuller-related writing, and the phrasing matches his idiom (serendipity as method, 'precession'). I cannot place it in a specific book from memory — some collections point to his poetic works of the late 1960s/early 1970s, but I will not assert a title I cannot confirm. Attribution is stable and plausible; the primary source is unlocated.

The formulation is characteristic of R. H. Blyth, whose 'Zen in English Literature and Oriental Classics' (1942) and multi-volume 'Zen and Zen Classics' argue exactly this — that Zen strips the world of symbolic overlay. I recall the line circulating as Blyth's and believe the attribution is genuine, but I cannot pin the volume or page from memory and will not guess between the two works.

This is a known misattribution. The joy/service triplet is a 20th-century reworking of Ellen Sturgis Hooper's short poem published in The Dial (1840): 'I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty; / I woke, and found that life was Duty.' The 'service was joy' variant has been floated under Tagore, Gandhi, and Kahlil Gibran in different collections — a spread that is itself diagnostic — and I know of no passage in Tagore's works containing it. Quote Investigator has treated this family of variants and traced it back to Hooper.
suggested_reattribution: Derived from Ellen Sturgis Hooper's 1840 poem ('I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty'); the joy/service wording has no known author

notes: Almost certainly not Tagore. The diction is modern colloquial American English ('my own version of an optimist', 'something terrific'), incompatible with Tagore's register in either Bengali or his own English renderings. I recognize this as a Joan Rivers line, widely quoted from her later interviews and her writing on resilience; the Tagore label appears to be a quote-site scrambling. I am confident it is not Tagore and reasonably confident it is Rivers, though I cannot name the specific book or interview.

Consistent with Tagore's metaphysics as expressed in 'Sadhana: The Realisation of Life' (1913) and 'The Religion of Man' (1931), and the attribution to him is stable across collections. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific text from memory, so I will not name a source. Plausible and uncontested but unverified.

A genuine and much-cited Tagore line on education, used institutionally in connection with Santiniketan and Visva-Bharati. It comes from his essays on education (collections such as 'Personality' (1917) and the 'A Poet's School' material are the usual pointers), but I cannot fix the exact essay from memory and will not guess. Strong, consistent attribution; specific citation unlocated.

earliest_print_source: The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, Rainer Maria Rilke, 1910
notes: From Rilke's novel 'Die Aufzeichnungen des Malte Laurids Brigge' (1910); Malte's observation that life offers no beginners' classes and demands the hardest thing immediately. Wording here matches the common English translations (Mitchell/Norton lineage). Confident in the work, so verified, though I cannot give a page.

earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, letter of 23 April 1903; published 1929, M. D. Herter Norton translation 1934
notes: From Letters to a Young Poet — the letter containing the 'ripening like a tree' passage, in which Rilke advises Kappus to grow quietly and seriously and warns against looking outward for answers. The English here is the Norton translation, whose slightly archaic syntax ('I do only want to advise you') matches. Confident in the work and the correspondence; letter number given from memory as the third.

earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, first letter, Paris, 17 February 1903; published 1929
notes: From the opening letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, immediately following the 'go into yourself' advice: if everyday life seems poor, the fault lies with the poet's insufficiency, not the life. One of the most securely sourced passages in the Rilke corpus.

Reads as authentic Rilke prose from his correspondence — the paradox of love increasing by being given, tied to flowers and children, is his register and imagery. It circulates widely through John J. L. Mood's anthology 'Rilke on Love and Other Difficulties' (1975), which gathers passages from the letters. I cannot identify which letter it comes from, so I will not cite one. Genuine-seeming but unsourced.

earliest_print_source: Letters to a Young Poet (Briefe an einen jungen Dichter), Rainer Maria Rilke, letter of 16 July 1903, Worpswede; published 1929
notes: The 'live the questions now' passage — the single best-known paragraph in Letters to a Young Poet, from the fourth letter. The wording here is a modern English rendering (locked rooms / books in a foreign language / live your way into the answer) and the ellipses are the compiler's, but the passage is unambiguously Rilke's.

earliest_print_source: Das Stunden-Buch (The Book of Hours), Rainer Maria Rilke, 1905; English in Rilke's Book of Hours: Love Poems to God, trans. Anita Barrows and Joanna Macy, 1996
notes: Closing lines of the poem beginning 'Gott spricht zu jedem nur, eh er ihn macht' ('God speaks to each of us as he makes us') from the Book of Hours. German: 'Lass dir Alles geschehn: Schönheit und Schrecken. / Man muss nur gehn: Kein Gefühl ist das fernste.' The familiar English wording, including 'No feeling is final', is the Barrows/Macy translation — worth noting since the line is often quoted as if bare Rilke.

A popular verse-shaped collage rather than a translation. One sentence has a real source: 'The future enters into us, in order to transform itself in us, long before it happens' is from Letters to a Young Poet (the letter of 12 August 1904 in the standard sequence). The surrounding lines — 'You must give birth to your images', 'the hour of new clarity' — do not correspond to any standard translation I can recall, and the arrangement into short lines is a modern editorial creation. Rilkean in origin but not a quotable Rilke text as it stands.

Plausibly from Rilke's wartime or post-war correspondence, where he links inner freedom to peace, and the sentence structure suggests translated German. I cannot place it in any letter or published work, and it does not appear in the well-trodden Letters to a Young Poet material. Attribution is uncontested but I have no evidence for it.

Attributed consistently to Ralph W. Gerard, the American neurophysiologist, and the thought matches his published interest in the biology of imagination and creative thinking (he wrote on 'the biological basis of imagination' in the mid-1940s). The attribution is stable and the author obscure enough that misattribution pressure is low — nobody invents a quote to hang on Ralph Gerard. Specific source unlocated.

Ralph Marston writes The Daily Motivator, a long-running series of short daily messages, and this is characteristic of that output in both voice and structure. Attribution to Marston is consistent wherever it appears. Individual Daily Motivator entries are dated but I cannot supply the date from memory, so no citation is given.

The 'What is Success?' passage — one of the most thoroughly documented Emerson misattributions. It originates with Bessie Anderson Stanley, whose prize-winning 1904 contest entry read 'He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'. The version here is a mid-20th-century expansion (the 'healthy child, a garden patch, a redeemed social condition' clauses are later accretions) that acquired Emerson's name in anthologies and greeting cards. It appears in no edition of Emerson's works. Emerson scholars and Quote Investigator both reject the attribution.
suggested_reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), in an evolved and expanded form by later hands

notes: Not found in Emerson's published works, journals, or letters as far as I know; the Emerson attribution is a 20th-century label with no textual support. The thought and structure track e. e. cummings closely: 'To be nobody-but-yourself in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight' (A Poet's Advice to Students, 1955). The circulating 'Emerson' sentence looks like a compressed rewording of cummings. Emerson is a misattribution magnet for self-reliance aphorisms precisely because 'Self-Reliance' makes the sentiment sound like his.
suggested_reattribution: Probably a compressed rewording of e. e. cummings, 'A Poet's Advice to Students' (1955)

notes: I believe this is genuine Emerson, but the canonical wording carries an extra word: 'A good intention clothes itself with sudden power.' The dropped 'sudden' suggests transmission through a quote collection rather than the text. My recollection places it in the Essays: First Series (1841) period, most likely 'Spiritual Laws', but I am not certain enough of the essay to cite it, and naming the wrong essay would be worse than naming none.

Genuine Emerson prose in my judgment — the passage continues '...all opportunities, strings of tension waiting to be struck', a cadence and image that belong to him and that no anthologist would invent. My recollection associates it with the later essays, 'Works and Days' in Society and Solitude (1870) being the most likely home, but I cannot confirm the essay and so leave the citation blank. Note the quote as given truncates the passage mid-thought.

From Emerson's first book, 'Nature' (1836), in the closing chapter 'Prospects'. The sentence is quoted accurately here and sits in the passage arguing that wisdom consists in perceiving the miraculous within the ordinary — the culminating movement of the essay.

Universally attributed to Emerson and entirely consistent with his thought, but I cannot place it in any essay, and its compact epigram form is the shape misattributions usually take. It may come from his journals, which are less well indexed in quote culture and therefore both a plausible home and a convenient one. Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be pointed to.

Circulates almost exclusively as Emerson, and occasionally as an anonymous proverb. I cannot locate it in his essays or journals, and the neat paradox reads more like a 19th- or 20th-century aphorism collection than like Emerson's sentence rhythm, which rarely lands this tidily. No evidence against him either — the honest verdict is that I do not know.

Doubtful as Emerson. I know of no passage in his published works containing it. In 20th-century usage the line is most strongly associated with the historian Charles A. Beard, who offered it as one of his 'lessons of history', and it was later used by Martin Luther King Jr.; both are transmitters rather than demonstrable origins. Related dark/stars proverbs predate all of them, so the true source may be proverbial. Treating this as unverified rather than reattributed because I cannot identify who said it first.

earliest_print_source: The Conduct of Life, Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1860
notes: Genuine Emerson, from The Conduct of Life (1860); my recollection places it in the essay 'Worship'. One wording note: the canonical text reads 'where every one hides his real character, and reveals it by hiding' — the quote here has 'his own character', a small corruption worth correcting against the printed text before promotion.
